pages.text: Reptiles

image.note: Cover: a lizard, a snake, a turtle and a crocodile

pages.text: Contents. The Scaled Ones / Cold Blood, Warm Sun / Snakes / Lizards / Turtles and Crocodiles / Living with Reptiles.

Bask on a warm rock, and you might meet one. Slip through the grass, glide through a river, or blink from a branch, and there they are: the reptiles, ancient, scaled, and strange. They ruled the earth in the age of the dinosaurs, and they are with us still. This is the story of the scaled ones, and the sunlit lives they lead.

image.note: Various reptiles basking and moving in the sun

pages.text: Snakes and lizards, turtles and crocodiles: at first they seem very different from one another. Yet they belong to the same great family, and share the same clever plan for living. Once you know their secret, the whole scaled kingdom begins to make sense.

What makes a reptile a reptile? First, its skin. A reptile is covered in scales, dry and tough, that protect it and hold in water, so it need not stay wet as a frog does. That scaly skin lets reptiles live in the driest, hottest places on earth, where softer animals would wither.

image.note: Close-up of a reptile's dry, scaly skin

pages.text: Most reptiles lay eggs, often with tough, leathery shells, hidden in a warm, safe place and left to hatch on their own. And nearly all reptiles have another thing in common, a thing that shapes their whole way of life: they are cold-blooded.

image.note: A reptile laying leathery eggs in a warm place

pages.text: Being cold-blooded does not mean a reptile's blood is cold. It means a reptile cannot warm itself from the inside, the way you can. Your body makes its own heat, and stays warm whatever the weather. A reptile cannot. It is only ever as warm as the world around it.

image.note: A reptile taking on the temperature around it

pages.text: So a reptile must borrow its warmth from the Sun. In the morning, cool and slow, it creeps out to bask on a warm rock, soaking up the heat until its body is warm enough to move quickly and hunt. This is why you so often see a lizard sunbathing, quite still: it is not being lazy. It is charging up.

image.note: A lizard basking on a sun-warmed rock

pages.text: There is a great advantage to this. Because a reptile makes no heat of its own, it needs very little food, far less than a warm animal of the same size. A big snake may eat only a few times a year. Borrowing warmth from the Sun is a wonderfully thrifty way to live.

image.note: A well-fed snake resting, needing little food

pages.text: Of all reptiles, snakes are perhaps the most misunderstood. They have no legs, and no ears, and never blink, for they have no eyelids. They move by rippling their whole long bodies, and can glide, climb, and even swim, with no limbs at all. It is a marvel of a design.

image.note: A snake moving in graceful ripples

pages.text: A snake flicks out its forked tongue not to sting, but to smell, tasting the air to find its way and its food. It can swallow prey far larger than its own head, for its jaws unhook to open astonishingly wide. Most snakes are shy and harmless, and would far rather slip away than meet you.

image.note: A snake tasting the air with its forked tongue

pages.text: Some snakes are dangerous, it is true, and should always be treated with care and respect, and left well alone. But snakes are not our enemies. They keep down the pests that eat our crops, and play their part in nature like every other animal. Understood, not feared, they are among the most remarkable creatures alive.

image.note: A snake at a respectful distance, doing its work in nature

pages.text: Lizards are the most common reptiles of all, and come in a wonderful range, from tiny ones that could sit on your finger to great ones as long as a canoe. Most are quick and watchful, darting after insects and basking in the sun on walls and rocks.

image.note: A variety of lizards, tiny to large

pages.text: Lizards have marvellous tricks. Some can change their colour to match their surroundings, or to show their mood, like the slow, swivel-eyed chameleon. Some can climb straight up glass on clever sticky feet. And many, if a hunter grabs their tail, can simply let the tail drop off and wriggle free, growing a new one later.

image.note: A chameleon changing colour, a gecko on glass

pages.text: Turtles and tortoises carry their homes on their backs, a hard shell they can pull into for safety. They are slow, but wonderfully long-lived: some tortoises live longer than any other animal on land, older than your grandparents, older even than their grandparents. A tortoise may see a hundred years and more.

image.note: A tortoise with its shell, looking very old and wise

pages.text: Crocodiles and their cousins are the giants of the reptile world, and the closest living relatives of the dinosaurs. They lurk, still as logs, in rivers and swamps, and have changed very little in millions of years. They are fierce hunters, and are best watched from a safe and respectful distance.

image.note: A crocodile lying still as a log in a river

pages.text: Reptiles have been on earth far longer than we have, since long before the dinosaurs. They survived when the great dinosaurs did not, and they live on today in nearly every warm land on earth. They ask only for sun to warm them and a place to live, and they harm us far less than we sometimes fear.

So the next time you see a lizard basking on a wall, or read of a snake or a great old tortoise, remember what they are: ancient, scaled survivors, borrowing their warmth from the Sun, going about lives that have barely changed since the age of giants. The scaled ones were here long before us, and they are wonders still.

image.note: A child watching a basking lizard with new respect

pages.text: Words to know. Reptile: a scaly, cold-blooded animal, most of which lay eggs. Scales: the dry, tough covering of a reptile. Cold-blooded: warmed by the surroundings, not from within. Basking: lying in the sun to warm up. Chameleon: a lizard that can change its colour.

From the sunbathing lizard to the ancient tortoise, reptiles show one clever way to live. Our living world is full of others, in the frozen poles, the deep rivers, and the busy machines we build. Which will you explore next?
